The earliest creatures are still very viable and they have been given updated movesets that make them even more viable. For example, a water-type creature can learn a defensive move, making him very tough to take out with physical moves. Some key differences between the earliest generation and the newer generation:   1) Attacks are now classified as *physical* or *special* based on the move itself, not the move's type. For example, in the early generations, all water-type moves were special, meaning they used the creature's special attack to determine how hard they hit. Now, some water-type moves are special and some are physical. A strong physical water-type move and a strong special water-type move exist.   2) The type matchup chart has changed. Dark, Steel, and Fairy types have been added and some other relationships have been modified. You can find a good type chart online.   3) Technical machines are now infinite-use. Once you receive a TM, you can use it an infinite amount of times.   4) There are a shit-ton more creatures. Over 700. You won't encounter all 700 in your game normally, but don't feel bad if you get overwhelmed a bit. A lot of times you can guess what type or types it is. Water types are usually blue and are found near the ocean/rivers/lakes/etc. Fire types are usually red, ground and rock types are found in caves, etc etc etc. Catch as many as you can and then look in your encyclopedia to see their specific type. Or you can just look online, but I imagine it's a pain to have to do that for every other battle.   5) The newest games have a rather overpowered experience share, meaning that if you only use three or four creatures throughout the game they will soon be WAY overleveled. Feel free to change out your team frequently. It doesn't take long to bring a new lower-leveled creature up to a respectable level.

Most people, as they age, start accumulating assets and wealth. A house, a car or two, a little bit of money in the bank, some money saved for retirement, etc. You start to become someone who *has* rather than your previous state of someone that *has not.* Much (not all) of a certain political ideology is based around not making those that *have* support those that *have not* more than their share. Which makes sense. If you've worked hard for what you have, and most likely been fucked over a few times by taxes, your job, insurance, etc, what money you have left, you are interested in keeping as much of it as you can. When you are young, you don't have a lot. So a lot of the government programs that benefit the less wealthy benefit you. So you tend to support those. Note that there isn't anything fundamentally wrong with either ideology. It's just where your priorities lie at that point in time, and this varies greatly from person to person. There are tons of people from one political spectrum wealthy and tons from the other poor. Sidenote: A big misconception is that one side opposes the government spending in all things. In actuality, most government programs tend to not be point of contention between different worldviews. Things like public services, police, funding for education, highway improvements, etc. are supported by both ideologies. The ones that are points of contention tend to be those that benefit a specific group of people rather than the vast majority of citizens. Like I said before, there isn't anything fundamentally wrong with either view. It's just a disagreement of opinion between two groups of people that are both rational and reasonable human beings.
